danish.title: Ellevte bog (1812) — Kapitel 13
paragraphs: Lørdag den enogtredivte august var alt i familien Rostovs hus på den anden ende. Alle dørene stod åbne, alle møblerne blev båret ud eller flyttet rundt, og spejlene og billederne var taget ned. Der stod kufferter i værelserne, og hø, indpakningspapir og reb lå spredt overalt. Bønderne og husslaverne, der bar tingene ud, trådte tungt hen over parketgulvene. Gården var fuld af bondevogne, nogle læsset højt og allerede snøret fast, andre stadig tomme.

Stemmerne og fodtrinene fra de mange tjenestefolk og bønderne, der var kommet med vognene, genlød, mens de råbte til hinanden i gården og i huset. Greven havde været ude siden morgenstunden. Grevinden havde fået hovedpine af al støjen og opstandelsen og lå i den nye dagligstue med en eddikekompres på panden. Petja var ikke hjemme; han var taget hen for at besøge en ven, med hvem han agtede at skaffe sig en overførsel fra militsen til den aktive hær. Sonja var i balsalen og førte tilsyn med pakningen af glas og porcelæn. Natasja sad på gulvet i sit ryddede værelse med kjoler, bånd og sjaler spredt omkring sig, stirrede stift på gulvet og holdt den gamle balkjole (allerede gået af mode), som hun havde båret til sit første bal i Petersborg, i hænderne.

Natasja skammede sig over at lave ingenting, når alle andre havde travlt, og havde flere gange den morgen forsøgt at tage fat, men hendes hjerte var ikke med, og hun hverken kunne eller vidste, hvordan man gør noget, med mindre det var med hele sit hjerte og al sin kraft. En stund havde hun stået ved siden af Sonja, mens porcelænet blev pakket, og forsøgt at hjælpe, men gav snart op og gik hen til sit værelse for at pakke sine egne ting. I begyndelsen morede det hende at give kjoler og bånd væk til tjenestepigerne, men da dét var gjort, og det, der var tilbage, stadig skulle pakkes, fandt hun det kedeligt.

»Dunjasja, du pakker! Det gør du vel nok, søde?« Og da Dunjasja villigt lovede at gøre det hele for hende, satte Natasja sig på gulvet, tog sin gamle balkjole og faldt i drømmeri, der slet ikke havde noget at gøre med det, der burde have optaget hendes tanker. Hun blev vækket af sin dagdrøm af snakken fra tjenestepigerne i naborummet (som var deres) og lyden af deres hastige skridt hen mod bagtrappen. Natasja rejste sig og kiggede ud ad vinduet. En uhyre lang række vogne fulde af sårede mænd var standset i gaden.
Husholderske, den gamle barnepige, kokkene, kuskene, stuepigerne, lakajer, postilloner og køkkendrenge stod ved porten og stirrede på de sårede.
Natasja kastede et rent lommetørklæde over sit hår, holdt en flig af det i hver hånd og gik ud på gaden.

Den tidligere husholderske, gamle Mavra Kuzminitjna, var trådt ud af mængden ved porten, gået hen til en vogn med et halvtag af bastmåtter og talte med en bleg, ung officer, der lå derinde. Natasja trådte et par skridt frem og standsede genert, stadig holdende sit lommetørklæde, og lyttede til, hvad husholdersken sagde.
»Så De har ingen i Moskva?« sagde hun. »De ville have det mere behageligt et sted i et hus... i vores for eksempel... familien rejser.«

»Jeg ved ikke, om det ville være tilladt,« svarede officeren med svag stemme. »Dér er vores kommandant... spørg ham,« og han pegede på en svær major, der kom gående tilbage langs gaden forbi rækken af vogne.
Natasja kiggede med forskræmte øjne på den sårede officers ansigt og gik straks hen for at møde majoren.
»Må de sårede bo i vores hus?« spurgte hun.
Majoren løftede hånden til kasketten med et smil.
»Hvem ønsker De, frøken?« sagde han og kneb øjnene sammen med et smil.

Natasja gentog stille sit spørgsmål, og hendes ansigt og hele hendes væsen var så alvorligt, skønt hun stadig holdt fligene af sit lommetørklæde, at majoren holdt op med at smile, og efter nogen betænkning — som om han overvejede, i hvor høj grad tingen var mulig — svarede bekræftende.
»Åh ja, hvorfor ikke? Det må de gerne,« sagde han.
Med en let hovedbøjning trådte Natasja hurtigt tilbage til Mavra Kuzminitjna, der stod og talte medfølende med officeren.
»Det er i orden. Han siger, de må!« hviskede Natasja.

Vognen med officeren blev drejet ind i Rostovernes gård, og snesevis af vogne med sårede mænd begyndte, på byboernes indbydelse, at dreje ind i gårdene og holde ved indgangene til husene i Povarskaja-gaden. Natasja var tydeligvis glad for at have med nye mennesker at gøre uden for sit daglige livs vante rammer. Hun og Mavra Kuzminitjna forsøgte at få så mange af de sårede som muligt ind i deres gård.
»Din far må dog fortælles det,« sagde Mavra Kuzminitjna.
»Det er lige meget, det er lige meget, hvad gør det? En enkelt dag kan vi rykke ind i dagligstuen. De kan få hele vores halvdel af huset.«
»Jamen, frøken, De finder da også på ting! Selv om vi anbringer dem i sidefløjen, i mandfolkerummet eller barnepigernes stue, må vi spørge om lov.«
»Godt, jeg skal nok spørge.«
Natasja løb ind i huset og gik på tåspidser gennem den halvåbne dør ind i dagligstuen, hvor der lugtede af eddike og Hoffmanns dråber.
»Sover du, Mama?«
»Åh, hvad søvn —?« sagde grevinden, der vågnede, netop som hun var ved at glide ind i en døs.

»Mama, skat!« sagde Natasja og knælede ved sin mor og bragte sit ansigt tæt til moderens. »Jeg er ked af det, tilgiv mig, jeg gør det aldrig igen; jeg vækkede dig! Mavra Kuzminitjna har sendt mig: de har bragt nogle sårede her — officerer. Vil du lade dem komme ind? De har ingen steder at gå hen. Jeg vidste, du ville lade dem komme ind!« sagde hun hurtigt, alt i ét åndedrag.
»Hvad for nogen officerer? Hvem har de bragt? Jeg forstår ikke noget af det,« sagde grevinden.
Natasja lo, og grevinden smilede også svagt.
»Jeg vidste, at du ville give lov... så jeg fortæller dem det,« og efter at have kysset sin mor rejste Natasja sig og gik mod døren.
I entréen mødte hun sin far, der var vendt hjem med dårlige nyheder.
»Vi er blevet for længe!« sagde greven med ufrivillig ærgrelse. »Klubben er lukket, og politiet rejser.«
»Papa, er det i orden — jeg har inviteret nogle af de sårede ind i huset?« sagde Natasja.

»Selvfølgelig,« svarede han adspredt. »Det er ikke det, det handler om. Jeg beder dig om ikke at give dig af med småting nu, men hjælpe med at pakke, og i morgen skal vi af sted, af sted, af sted!...«
Og greven gav en lignende ordre til hovmesteren og tjenestefolkene.

Ved middagen fortalte Petja, der var kommet hjem, dem de nyheder, han havde hørt. Han sagde, at folk havde hentet våben i Kreml, og at skønt Rostoptjins opslag havde sagt, at han ville give signal to eller tre dage i forvejen, var ordren bestemt allerede givet om, at alle skulle møde bevæbnede ved Tre Bakker i morgen, og at der ville blive et stort slag dér.

Grevinden så med frygtsom rædsel på sin søns ivrige, begejstrede ansigt, da han sagde dette. Hun indså, at hvis hun sagde et ord om, at han ikke skulle gå til kamp (hun vidste, at han nød tanken om det forestående slag), ville han sige noget om mænd, ære og fædrelandet — noget meningsløst, mandligt og stædigt, som der ikke ville være nogen modsigelse mod, og hendes planer ville blive ødelagt; og så, i håb om at arrangere afrejsen inden da og tage Petja med som familiens beskytter og forsvarer, svarede hun ham ikke, men kaldte efter middagen greven til side og bønfaldt ham under tårer om at tage hende bort hurtigt, allerede den nat, om muligt. Med en kvindes ufrivillige, kærlige list, sagde hun, der indtil da ikke havde vist nogen uro, at hun ville dø af skræk, hvis de ikke rejste den nat. Uden noget påskud var hun nu bange for alting.

english.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: On Saturday, August 31, everything in the Rostov house seemed topsy-turvy. All the doors were open, all the furniture was being carried out or rearranged, and the mirrors and pictures had been taken down. Trunks stood in the rooms, and hay, wrapping paper, and rope were scattered about. The peasants and house servants carrying things out trod heavily on the parquet floors. The yard was crowded with peasant carts — some loaded high and already roped up, others still empty.

The voices and footsteps of the many servants and the peasants who'd come with the carts echoed through the yard and house as they shouted to one another. The count had been out since morning. The countess, with a headache from all the noise and chaos, lay in the new sitting room with a vinegar compress on her forehead. Petya wasn't home — he'd gone to see a friend about getting a transfer from the militia to the active army. Sonya was in the ballroom overseeing the packing of glassware and china. Natasha sat on the floor of her dismantled room amid scattered dresses, ribbons, and scarves, staring at the floor and holding in her hands the old ball gown — already out of fashion — that she'd worn to her first Petersburg ball.

Natasha was ashamed of doing nothing when everyone else was so busy. Several times that morning she'd tried to help, but her heart wasn't in it, and she simply didn't know how to do anything without giving it her whole heart and soul. For a while she'd stood beside Sonya while the china was being packed and tried to assist, but soon gave up and went to her room to pack her own things. At first she enjoyed giving away dresses and ribbons to the maids, but when that was done and what remained still had to be packed, she found it tedious.

"Dunyasha, you pack it! You will, won't you, dear?" And when Dunyasha cheerfully promised to do it all, Natasha sat down on the floor, took her old ball gown, and drifted into a daydream entirely unrelated to what should have occupied her thoughts. She was roused by the chatter of the maids in the next room and their hurried footsteps toward the back porch. Natasha got up and looked out the window. An enormously long row of carts full of wounded men had stopped in the street.
The housekeeper, the old nurse, the cooks, coachmen, maids, footmen, postilions, and kitchen boys all stood at the gate, staring at the wounded.
Natasha, throwing a clean handkerchief over her hair and holding an end in each hand, went out into the street.

The former housekeeper, old Mavra Kuzminichna, had stepped out from the crowd at the gate and approached a cart with a hood made of bark matting. She was talking to a pale young officer who lay inside. Natasha came a few steps closer and stopped shyly, still holding her handkerchief, listening to what the housekeeper was saying.
"So you have nobody in Moscow?" she was saying. "You'd be more comfortable in a house somewhere — in ours, for instance. The family is leaving."
"I don't know if it would be allowed," the officer replied weakly. "There's our commanding officer — ask him," and he pointed to a stout major walking back along the street past the line of carts.
Natasha glanced with frightened eyes at the wounded officer's face and immediately went to meet the major.
"May the wounded men stay in our house?" she asked.
The major raised his hand to his cap with a smile.
"Which one would you like, miss?" he said, squinting and smiling.

Natasha quietly repeated her question, and her face and whole manner were so serious — though she was still holding the ends of her handkerchief — that the major stopped smiling and, after a moment's reflection, as if weighing whether it could be arranged, answered in the affirmative.
"Oh yes, why not? They may," he said.
With a slight nod, Natasha hurried back to Mavra Kuzminichna, who was still talking sympathetically to the officer.
"They may! He says they may!" she whispered.

The cart carrying the officer was turned into the Rostovs' yard, and at the invitation of the townspeople, dozens of carts with wounded men began pulling into the yards and drawing up at the entrances of houses along Povarskaya Street. Natasha was clearly pleased to be dealing with new people outside her ordinary routine. She and Mavra Kuzminichna tried to get as many wounded as possible into their yard.
"Your papa should be told, though," said Mavra Kuzminichna.
"Never mind, never mind — what does it matter? For one day we can move into the drawing room. They can have our whole half of the house."
"Really now, young lady, the ideas you get! Even if we put them in the wing — the men's room or the nurse's room — we still need permission."
"Well, I'll ask."
Natasha ran into the house and went on tiptoe through the half-open door into the sitting room, where there was a smell of vinegar and Hoffmann's drops.
"Are you asleep, Mama?"
"What sleep?" said the countess, waking up just as she was drifting off.

"Mama, darling!" said Natasha, kneeling by her mother and bringing her face close. "I'm sorry — forgive me — I'll never do it again. I woke you up! Mavra Kuzminichna sent me — they've brought wounded men here, officers. Will you let them stay? They have nowhere to go. I knew you'd say yes!" she said all in one breath.
"What officers? Who's been brought? I don't understand anything," said the countess.
Natasha laughed, and the countess smiled slightly too.
"I knew you'd give permission — so I'll tell them," and, kissing her mother, Natasha jumped up and went to the door.
In the hall she met her father, who had returned with bad news.
"We've stayed too long!" the count said with involuntary irritation. "The Club is closed and the police are leaving."
"Papa, is it all right? I've invited some of the wounded into our house," said Natasha.
"Of course, of course," he answered absently. "That's not the point. Please stop fussing with trifles and help with the packing. Tomorrow we must go — go, go!"
And the count gave similar orders to the major-domo and servants.

At dinner, Petya came home and told them his news. He said people had been collecting weapons at the Kremlin, and though Rostopchin's broadsheet had promised two or three days' warning, the order had already been given for everyone to go armed to the Three Hills tomorrow — there was going to be a big battle there.

The countess looked with timid horror at her son's eager, excited face. She realized that if she said a word about his not going to the battle (she knew how much he relished the thought), he would say something about men, honor, and the fatherland — something senseless, masculine, and unanswerable — and her plans would be ruined. So, hoping to arrange to leave before then and take Petya along as their protector and defender, she said nothing. After dinner, she took the count aside and, in tears, begged him to take her away — that very night if possible. With a woman's instinctive, loving cunning, she who until then had shown no alarm now said she would die of fright if they didn't leave that very night. Without pretending, she was now afraid of everything.
